races.long_description: Senator Tommy Tuberville, the Republican firebrand and former Auburn football coach, is facing Doug Jones, the Democrat he ousted in 2020. Mr. Tuberville’s campaign has been defined by his alliance with President Trump and a steady drumbeat of anti-Muslim and anti-immigrant messaging, while Mr. Jones leaned on his Senate record and civil rights work.

Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, 37, a former state lawmaker, is trying to become Alaska’s youngest governor ever and its first Democratic one since 1998. Under Alaska’s top-four ranked-choice voting system, he faces three Republicans: Bernadette Wilson, owner of a garbage collection company; Treg Taylor, a former attorney general; and Dave Bronson, a former Anchorage mayor. Ms. Wilson has President Trump’s endorsement.

Gov. Katie Hobbs of Arizona, the Democratic incumbent, is fighting to keep control of the desert battleground’s highest office. Ms. Hobbs, a moderate, is facing Representative Andy Biggs, a Trump-endorsed former chair of the far-right House Freedom Caucus who’s backed by Turning Point USA.

Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders, a Republican, is heavily favored to win a second term. Ms. Sanders, who served as President Trump’s press secretary during his first term, is facing Fred Love, a Democratic state senator.
Xavier Becerra, a Democrat who served as secretary of health and human services in the Biden administration, is favored to defeat Steve Hilton, a former Fox News host endorsed by President Trump.

Colorado, a onetime swing state that has veered to the left, is expected to elect Phil Weiser, the state’s Democratic attorney general, as its next governor. Republicans were deeply divided over their own candidate, Victor Marx, a ministry leader and political neophyte.

Gov. Ned Lamont, a Democrat, is seeking a third consecutive term, a feat accomplished only once before in the state. His Republican challenger, Ryan Fazio, a state senator from Greenwich, is grappling with fierce political headwinds. No one in his party has won a statewide election in 20 years.

Byron Donalds, the Republican backed by President Trump, is vying to continue the party’s dominance in the governor’s mansion. A victory would make him Florida’s first Black governor. He faces David Jolly, a former Republican congressman who became a Democrat last year. No Democrat has held the governorship in Florida since the late 1990s.

Rick Jackson, a health care executive, is aiming to hold the governorship for Republicans in politically mixed Georgia. He is facing Keisha Lance Bottoms, a Democrat and a former mayor of Atlanta. The Republican incumbent, Gov. Brian Kemp, was barred by term limits from running again.

Gov. Josh Green of Hawaii, a Democrat who led his state during the Maui wildfires in 2023, is heavily favored to win a second term in a place where Republicans are rarely competitive in statewide races. Gary Cordery, a businessman, is the Republican nominee.
Gov. Brad Little, a Republican, is seeking a third term in a reliably conservative state. Terri Pickens, a lawyer, is the Democratic nominee.

Gov. JB Pritzker, a billionaire Democrat who is believed to be weighing a run for president, is seeking a third term in his solidly Democratic state. Mr. Pritzker, a vocal critic of President Trump, is facing a rematch of his 2022 race with Darren Bailey, a Republican former state senator.

In a state that has been controlled by Republicans for close to a decade, a surprisingly competitive race for governor has unfolded between Rob Sand, the Democratic state auditor, and Zach Lahn, a Republican supported by the MAHA movement.

Republicans see Kansas as an opportunity to flip the governorship on an otherwise foreboding electoral map. Ty Masterson, the Republican nominee and president of the Kansas Senate, has aligned himself with President Trump. State Senator Cindy Holscher, who emerged from a fractious Democratic primary, is trying to hold the seat for her party.

Hannah Pingree, a Democrat and former Maine House speaker, has maintained a steady lead in polls over Bobby Charles, a conservative Republican. The winner will succeed Gov. Janet Mills, a term-limited Democrat whose conflict with President Trump raised her national profile.

Gov. Wes Moore, a Democrat and possible future presidential candidate, is a heavy favorite in his bid for a second term. He is facing a rematch with Dan Cox, a Republican former state legislator who lost to Mr. Moore by a large margin four years ago.

Gov. Maura Healey, a Democrat and a vocal critic of President Trump, is seeking a second term in her solidly Democratic state. Mike Minogue, a former medical technology executive with conservative views, is the Republican nominee.

Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson is trying to keep the governor’s office in Democratic hands for a third straight term. She faces Representative John James, a Republican from suburban Detroit, in a state where voters swing regularly between parties.

Senator Amy Klobuchar, a Democrat, entered the governor’s race early this year after Gov. Tim Walz suspended his campaign for a third term amid a scandal over social services fraud. She is favored to defeat Lisa Demuth, the Republican speaker of the Minnesota House.

Gov. Jim Pillen, a Republican, is facing a surprisingly competitive re-election race in a state that has not elected a Democrat as governor in more than 30 years but where many voters are frustrated with federal agricultural policies. His opponent, former State Senator Lynne Walz, has pitched herself to voters as a different kind of Democrat, often noting her Christian faith and her childhood on a hog farm.

Joe Lombardo, a relatively moderate Republican, is looking to win re-election in one of the nation’s most competitive races for governor. He faces the state’s attorney general, Democrat Aaron Ford, who has sought to tie Mr. Lombardo to President Trump. Mr. Ford would be Nevada’s first Black governor.

Gov. Kelly Ayotte, a Republican who served in the U.S. Senate, is seeking re-election, while her challenger, Cinde Warmington, a Democratic lawyer and former lobbyist, argues that Ms. Ayotte would enable “more Trump chaos” in a second term.

Deb Haaland, the former Democratic congresswoman and interior secretary, is looking to become the nation’s first female Native American governor. A Republican former mayor, Gregg Hull, is mounting a long-shot challenge notable for the unusual promise he made at its outset: No negative campaigning.

After winning by a closer-than-expected margin four years ago, Gov. Kathy Hochul is hoping that anger with President Trump will turn out Democratic voters and help her comfortably secure a second term over her Republican opponent, Bruce Blakeman, the Nassau County executive.

In an expensive and markedly bitter race, Vivek Ramaswamy, who made millions in pharmaceutical start-ups and briefly ran for president in 2024, is running against Dr. Amy Acton, who was the state’s chief public health officer in the early days of the Covid pandemic.

Mike Mazzei, a former state senator, emerged from a competitive Republican primary with President Trump’s endorsement and is favored to hold the open seat for his party. But Democrats, whose candidates are usually trounced in statewide races, have invested in the race and expressed hope that their nominee, State Representative Cyndi Munson, could be competitive.

In a rematch of 2022, Democratic incumbent Tina Kotek faces Christine Drazan, a conservative Republican state legislator. Ms. Kotek’s low approval rating and the state’s slow recovery from the pandemic have made this a closer campaign than the state’s demographics would suggest.

Josh Shapiro, a Democrat and a potential 2028 presidential contender, is running for re-election against Stacy Garrity, the state treasurer and a retired colonel in the U.S. Army Reserve. With healthy approval numbers statewide, Mr. Shapiro has kept a formidable lead in the polls.

Helena Foulkes, a Democrat who is a former CVS executive, defeated Gov. Dan McKee in her party’s primary to establish herself as a strong favorite in the general election. Her opponents include Aaron Guckian, a Republican, and Ken Block, a businessman running as an independent.

Gov. Larry Rhoden, a Republican, emerged from a competitive primary as a strong favorite to be elected to a full term. Mr. Rhoden, who had been lieutenant governor, ascended to the state’s highest office last year when former Gov. Kristi Noem joined President Trump’s cabinet. He is facing Dan Ahlers, a Democrat who previously served in the State Legislature.

Senator Marsha Blackburn, a Trump ally, is the front-runner to become Tennessee’s first female governor. She faces a number of challengers, including Jerri Green, a Democratic Memphis councilwoman. There are also two surprisingly robust independent challenges from Lauren Pinkston, an academic, and David Hatley, a businessman.

Greg Abbott, the well-moneyed, longtime governor of Texas, is up against Gina Hinojosa, a state lawmaker who has pulled ahead in the polls in recent weeks. No matter the outcome, it will be record-setting: A win for Mr. Abbott would mean a fourth term as governor, a first in Texas history; a win for Ms. Hinojosa would mean the state’s first Hispanic governor.
Gov. Phil Scott, a moderate Republican seeking a sixth term, is facing Amanda Janoo, a progressive Democrat and a political newcomer whose campaign has picked up unexpected momentum.

Representative Tom Tiffany, a Republican with close ties to President Trump, is facing David Crowley, a Democrat and the Milwaukee County executive. Mr. Crowley is hoping to keep the seat in Democratic hands and help his party win a trifecta in Wisconsin.

State Senator Eric Barlow, a Republican who defeated a candidate endorsed by President Trump in the primary election, is widely expected to hold the governorship for his party. Ken Casner, the Democratic nominee, is a military veteran who runs a retail shop and cafe.

content.text: The string of victories that secured Democratic control of the Senate
in Iowa, Kansas, Texas, Ohio, and both North and South Carolina
would have been unimaginable a year ago, in a reflection of how President Trump’s war with Iran and economic policies dramatically expanded the battlefield
Democrats began the cycle with a Senate map that was stacked against them
But voter dissatisfaction with soaring gas prices and a high cost of living
as well as a number of weak Republican candidates
helped the party make inroads into territory that was long considered solidly Republican

Republicans in Texas tried to motivate voters by telling them that the stakes of the midterms were existential for the future of the nation. It became a refrain for Ken Paxton as he traveled the state. “I’m not exaggerating when I say if we lose Texas, we lose America,” he told Republicans as part of his closing message. In the end, the pitch did not succeed.

content.text: Representative Ashley Hinson, the Republican nominee for Senate in Iowa, said she called her opponent, Josh Turek, to congratulate him on his victory. “It is time to put politics aside, dial down the rhetoric,” she said.

Adam Hamilton’s victory in the Senate race in Kansas is historic, but it is not the only contest that Democrats in the state are watching tonight. The party is also hoping to hold the governorship and unseat Attorney General Kris Kobach. Democrats hold very narrow leads in both of those races as we wait on a few rural counties to report their results.
The lack of complaints about a “rigged” election from the president and his allies is remarkable but also not surprising given the level of blowout Republicans were handed tonight.

Democrats have flipped at least five Senate seats tonight in states Donald Trump won by more than 10 percentage points just two years ago. That kind of partisan shift between a presidential and midterm election — in this many states — hasn’t been seen since 1986, when Democrats flipped eight Senate seats to regain Senate control.
Democrats have won control of the U.S. Senate, according to
New York Times projections
. We can make this projection because the Democrat
Josh Turek has won in Iowa
, according to our projections, giving Democrats the 51 seats they need to overcome Vice President JD Vance’s tie-breaking vote in the Senate.

The factors that contributed to the Democrats’ stunning victories in Texas will be analyzed in the days ahead as more becomes known about the voters who propelled Democrats to victory. But one thing appeared clear: Republicans were not helped by President Trump’s repeated visits to the state. Paxton tied his fate closely to the president, appearing with him at each stop. Abbott, too, has been a staunch defender of the president’s policies. The losses appeared likely to weaken the party’s MAGA wing, renewing a bitter internal battle that has consumed Texas Republicans for years.

Representative Suzan DelBene, Democrat of Washington State and the chairwoman of the DCCC, took the stage at the official watch party in the nation’s capital for House Democrats. “We won the majority, district by district, with amazing candidates,” she said. “They understand their job is representative, not rubber stamp.”

Representative Katherine Clark of Massachusetts, the no. 2 House Democrat set to make history as the first female majority leader next year, spoke next. “As we have traveled this country, it’s the story of the American people. It’s the stories of the families who used the metaphors of drowning: drowning in bills, not being able to keep their head above water,” she said.

The crowd then chanted “Speaker Jeffries!” as Representative Hakeem Jeffries, Democrat of New York and minority leader, took the stage. “America is back,” he says. “Today begins the great American comeback.”

Ken Paxton has conceded his race for the U.S. Senate in Texas. Paxton, a Republican attorney general who came into the race as the favorite, spoke for about two minutes. He said he was grateful to have served as attorney general for 12 years. “As soon as I’m out of office, I’ve still got a lot of friends in Texas,” he said. Paxton, a low-key speaker, did not seem overly emotional. After he finished speaking, supporters hugged and shook hands, clutching drinks in their hands. James Talarico, Paxton’s opponent, will be the first Democrat elected by Texas to the Senate since 1988 — the year before Talarico was born.

One of James Talarico’s biggest donors, the billionaire Democrat Reid Hoffman, is out with a statement to me about Talarico’s win — and taking a shot at his business rival, Elon Musk. “A lot of people said Texas was a pipe dream. But James Talarico met Texans where they are with a vision for a more hopeful and secure future. By putting people first, he helped build one of the largest movements in American politics to overcome a single individual willing to spend more than $200 million to defeat him,” Hoffman told The Times. Hoffman gave $16.5 million to the main pro-Talarico super PAC.
Hannah Pingree, a former Maine House speaker who emerged from a chaotic ranked-choice primary as the Democratic nominee for governor, won the election, The Associated Press reported.

She beat Bobby Charles, a conservative Republican and former State Department official who had ​r​ecently emphasized several policy differences with President Trump. Pingree was policy director for Gov. Janet Mills, the term-limited Democrat she will replace. Her mother, Chellie Pingree, has long represented southern Maine in Congress.
But Hannah Pingree downplayed her connections, peppering the state with signs for “Hannah” and stressing plans to make health care and housing more affordable.

In the Times interview, Trump defended some of his most unpopular policies. He said he did not regret his decision to go to war with Iran, and believed that voters agreed with his position. But he acknowledged that they were unhappy with gas prices. “They don’t mind the Iran, but they probably weren’t happy with the oil prices.​”

Gina Hinojosa just took the stage to thunderous cheers. “ We showed anything is possible,” she said. “It never bothered me that they doubted me. It bothered me that they doubted us.” She said the sitting governor, Greg Abbott, offered to help her with the transition of power. She thanked him for his service.

After a roughly seven-minute concession speech, Gov. Greg Abbott has stayed at his watch party to thank his supporters. Some of those here are embracing, several have headed to the bar, and others appear to be still processing the news. A cover band had just finished its set before the governor suddenly appeared in the room and took the stage to speak. They did not know that Abbott had already called his challenger to concede the race until they heard the news from the governor.

The sea change that is taking place in Texas is hard to overstate. Many here expected that James Talarico could beat a flawed candidate like Ken Paxton. Few if any were anticipating taking out Gov. Greg Abbott after three terms. And it appears that other statewide offices could fall to Democrats as well. The state is being transformed politically in ways that few have contemplated until tonight.

President Trump, in a phone call with The New York Times, said that he believed Republicans suffered losses tonight because he was not on the ballot. “I really think the fact that I wasn’t on the ballot was the single biggest issue,” Trump said.

I’m here at James Talarico’s election night watch party, where the mood could not be more elated. Everywhere people cannot believe what is happening. Democrats started the night hopeful but cautious, having been let down so many times before. Now, they are celebrating.

The Associated Press has not called the race for Texas governor. A win for Gina Hinojosa, a Democratic lawmaker from the Rio Grande Valley, would make her the first Hispanic governor in Texas, a state where Latinos make the largest population. The mood at her election night party at Assembly Hall in Austin, Texas became electric almost as soon as the results started coming in.

Ken Paxton’s loss is a dramatic political failure for Elon Musk, who spent over $212 million to boost Paxton. Musk spent $158 million that effectively financed a barrage of anti-Talarico ads, and spent at least $44 million on a voter-contact campaign in the state. There are a lot of reasons why Paxton lost, of course, and the national environment was brutal. But politics is a binary, and Mr. Musk’s candidate lost.

Speaker Mike Johnson, a Republican, has all but conceded that his party has lost the majority. Speaking at his watch party in Shreveport, La., he continued his campaign message by painting Democratic control of Congress as dangerous and “radical.”

“To every American disappointed by tonight’s results, I mean, I’m disappointed too. But we are never discouraged because we live in the greatest nation in the world,” he told the crowd as he vowed to continue to fight what he said would be a “socialist agenda” in Washington.

With the Senate race now called for James Talarico, and Governor Abbott calling to concede, Tuesday’s results mark a seismic shift in Texas politics. Republicans, after decades of statewide dominance, have lost their hold on the state, which now is about to enter a new and far more Democratic era. The Associated Press has not called the race for Abbott’s Democratic opponent, Gina Hinojosa.

Speaking to supporters in Rockland County, N.Y., Representative Mike Lawler is conceding to his Democratic opponent, Cait Conley. The New York Times has yet to accept a call in the race, which was one of the most closely watched and most expensive races in the country. Lawler has been a target of Democrats for years, but has managed to fend off stout challenges before.
“Despite the result, this was the best congressional campaign in the entire country, from start to finish,” Lawler said just now.

In Texas, Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat, is currently in the lead over Gov. Greg Abbott with about 60 percent of the vote counted. Counties with all their votes reported so far have shifted about 10 to 15 percentage points toward Hinojosa. In Kleberg, a majority-Hispanic rural county that Donald Trump won by 13 percentage points in 2024, Hinojosa is ahead by 10 points.

Gov. Greg Abbott of Texas said he had called his opponent, Gina Hinojosa, to concede the race for governor. Abbott noted that there are still votes to be counted, and the race has not been called.  “It has been the joy of my life to have the opportunity to be the governor of the great state of Texas,” he said.
Gov. Greg Abbott of Texas said he had called his Democratic opponent, Gina Hinojosa, to concede the race for governor. The race has not yet been called by The Associated Press.
For a sign of how seriously Republicans are struggling in their typical Southern strongholds, look no further than Louisiana.

Julia Letlow, the Republican nominee, is leading the race by more than 10 percentage points, but her margins may end up far tighter than the 20-percentage-point blowouts Republicans have come to expect in the state.

Acadiana, home to Louisiana’s Cajun communities, swung sharply to the left this year after decades as a reliable Republican stronghold. While Letlow can still claim victory in the region, she’s running behind President Trump’s 2024 margin by 20 percentage points or more in many of those parishes. Elsewhere in the state, Jamie Davis, the Democratic nominee, is outperforming Kamala Harris by double digits in every parish that has completed casting ballots.

content.text: Two of the most expensive races this election cycle were in Ohio, where groups spent heavily against the Democratic candidates.

In the governor’s race, Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign flooded the state with roughly $74 million worth of ads, according to AdImpact, a media tracking firm. A super PAC backing his bid for governor also pitched in another $63 million worth of ads. The campaign for Amy Acton, the Democrat candidate, spent only about $33 million on ads on her way to winning the race.

In the Senate race, the cryptocurrency industry spent more than $46 million on TV and digital ads to oppose Sherrod Brown and support Jon Husted. In 2024, that industry also spent tens of millions of dollars on ads to target Brown, who was then the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee and a critic of crypto. Despite the huge ad spend against him, Brown is leading Husted with roughly 85 percent of the expected vote in.

Peggy Flanagan, the Democratic nominee in Minnesota, is trailing in the Senate race against Michele Tafoya, but a vast majority of the votes in that state have yet to be reported, including in Hennepin and Ramsey counties in the Minneapolis-St. Paul metro area. Two of the largest in the state, these counties are expected to be very favorable for Flanagan.

President Trump won Iowa by 13 percentage points in 2024, but the Senate race there is a microcosm of Republicans’ rough night. Josh Turek, the Democrat, is getting just the kinds of shifts he needs across nearly the entirety of the state. That’s true in urban Democratic-leaning strongholds like Polk County, home to Des Moines, as well as rural Obama-Trump counties like Cerro Gordo.

Darline Graham, who was appointed to the Senate after the death of her brother, Lindsey, in July, said in her concession speech that it had been a difficult few months on the campaign trail. “I would trade this all a thousand times over to have my brother back, but God had a different plan,” she said. She thanked President Trump for his support in the race. “He loves this country dearly,” she said.

Representative Vicente Gonzalez, a Democrat, defeated Eric Flores, a Republican, in Texas’ 34th Congressional District, according to The Associated Press, a victory that suggests Latino voters in the region who had swung Republican in recent elections were frustrated over the cost of living and the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement.

Flores, a former federal prosecutor and Army veteran backed by President Trump, repeatedly attacked Gonzalez as ineffective in Washington while Gonzalez, in turn, portrayed Flores as being in lockstep with the president.
Texas 34th Congressional District Election Results ›

Senator John Cornyn, the Texas Republican who lost his re-election bid after President Trump backed Ken Paxton in the primary, congratulated James Talarico, the Democratic candidate, in a social media post. Though The Times has not yet called the race for Talarico, who is leading in the vote count, Cornyn said that he looked “forward to meeting him and offering my assistance with his transition as he prepares to serve Texans in the U.S. Senate.”

Voters in New York City approved five ballot proposals that were backed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, according to The Associated Press. The measures could help his efforts to build housing and expand outdoor dining and bike lanes. Opponents had argued that they would limit public input on projects.

Faces are getting longer at Ken Paxton’s watch party in Dallas. One man, upset about early votes in favor of Paxton’s Democratic rival for Senate, James Talarico, walked by the press and said loudly, “This is how countries go into revolution.”

Senator Darline Graham, the Republican who was defeated in a stunning upset in South Carolina, just took the stage at her watch party in Columbia, S.C. She said she had just gotten off the phone with Dr. Annie Andrews, her Democratic opponent, and congratulated her on becoming the first female senator elected in the state.“It is clear that we as conservatives have work to do, and that work starts tonight,” she said.

In Ohio, Sherrod Brown currently leads Senator Jon Husted by less than two percentage points. But the majority of the votes left to be tallied are in areas that have typically been more favorable to Democrats. The largest share of votes left are coming from Franklin County, home of Columbus, where Brown is currently leading by more than 30 percentage points.
Our election forecast considers a Brown victory very likely.
Democrats have now flipped six House seats held by Republicans, three of them in the critical presidential battleground state of Pennsylvania.

In South Carolina, Annie Andrews promises to be “an independent voice who will work with everyone” in the Senate. Without mentioning her defeated Republican opponent, she alludes to Darline Graham’s appointment and how it did not sit well with many voters. “Nobody in Washington recruited me to run,” Andrews said. “Nobody handed me a seat in the United States Senate. And nobody wrote me a script. I owe no one in Washington anything.”

Hundreds of supporters have been partying for hours waiting to celebrate Dr. Annie Andrews’s victory in the South Carolina Senate race. They greeted her to shouts of “Annie!” when she finally took the stage. “You have shown the nation what is possible,” she told them, noting she would be the first pediatrician in the Senate, and the first woman elected to the chamber from the state. (The interim Republican senator, Darline Graham, was appointed to the role.)
In the Kansas Senate race, Adam Hamilton has made substantial inroads in some critical counties. He is carrying his home base of
Johnson
County, which has mostly finished reporting, by 28 percentage points; in 2024, Kamala Harris won it by eight.
Wyandotte
, home to Kansas City and large shares of Black and Hispanic voters, shifted back left this year after moving right in 2024.
Hamilton is winning Wyandotte by 49 percentage points; in comparison, Harris won it by just 24. In
Lyon
, which Harris lost in 2024, Hamilton leads by eight percentage points, which is close to the nearly 10-point margin that Gov. Laura Kelly, a Democrat, won it by

Across the country, counties that have a majority of white working-class voters, a key component of President Trump’s base, have swung toward Democrats.

The group, which has overwhelmingly supported Republicans over the last decade, swung about 15 percentage points toward Democrats. In Iowa’s Dubuque County, where Trump won by nine percentage points in 2024, Josh Turek is ahead by five points. In our
polls
, we saw white working-class voters shifting away from Republicans.

Representative Rob Bresnahan Jr., a Pennsylvania Republican who emerged as one of the most active stock traders in Congress, was defeated by Paige Cognetti, the Democratic challenger, according to The Associated Press.

Cognetti, the mayor of Scranton, made Bresnahan’s stock trading a centerpiece of her pitch to voters, hammering him for profiting from trades while in office despite running on a pledge to ban the practice.

Bob Brooks, a victorious Democratic House candidate in Pennsylvania, was a rare progressive candidate who attracted early support in the primary from Democrats across the political spectrum, from Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont to Gov. Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania. The left is likely to point to his victory as another sign that populist policies can appeal in swing districts.

Thomas DiNapoli, a Democrat, is set to become the longest-serving comptroller in New York State history, defeating a Republican businessman, Joseph Hernandez, according to The Associated Press. DiNapoli, who has held the office for 20 years, faced his first competitive primary in June and defeated two challengers from the left.
He prides himself on being free of scandal. “Unlike every other position in the state government,” DiNapoli told The New York Times this spring, “I haven’t had to resign.”
